blocks.text: But many of the ancients also believed that in Ezech. XVII, 3. 7. the eagle is called מלא הנוצה and רב הנוצה on account of its talons. For this is rendered by the Greeks ὁ ἀετὸς πλήρης ὀνύχων [ho aetos plērēs onychōn], the eagle full of talons, and πολὺς ὄνυξι [polys onyxi], great in talons, or having many talons. The Arabic follows the same. Nor does the Syriac differ much in verse 3, ܡܠܝܢ ܛܦܪ̈ܘܗܝ, its talons are full, and in verse 7, ܣܓܝܐܢ ܛܦܪܘܗܝ its talons are many. For them, that is, נוצה is talon. But the Chaldee, Jerome and all the Hebrews more correctly explain it as feather or plumage. Indeed the Greeks themselves in Levit. I, 16. have σὺν τοῖς πτεροῖς [syn tois pterois] for בנצתא, and Theodotion σὺν τοῖς πτίλοις [syn tois ptilois]. For נצה means to fly, whence נצו they flew, or flew away, Thren. IV, 15., and נוצה feather or plumage, which lifts birds up to flight. This suits this passage better. For I, at least, cannot understand what an eagle full of talons, or with many talons, would be, since all eagles have the same number of talons. But an eagle is rightly said to be full of feathers, or to have many feathers, in contrast to the bald one ^{(2)}, of which Mich. I, 16. speaks: Enlarge thy baldness as the eagle. For at the onset of spring birds of prey are subject to the shedding of their feathers. This we call muer, that is, to change feathers. For so those speak who write on this subject. And this is precisely μουτεύειν [mouteuein] among the Greeks of a later age. Demetrius, Orneosophion, book 2, chapter 53: Ἐὰν δὲ βραδύνῃ εἰς τὸ μουτεῦσαι [Ean de bradynē eis to mouteusai]. Though proper words are not lacking, such as μαδίζεσθαι [madizesthai], πτεροῤῥυῆσαι [pterorrhyēsai], and ἀποβάλλειν τὰ πτερὰ [apoballein ta ptera], which the same writer uses. In Arabic you would say كرز [kariza] curiza. Alcamus: كرز البازي سقط ريشه [kariza al-bāzī saqaṭa rīshuhu] curiza albazi, that is, of the hawk, its plumage fell out. Whence كرز [kurraz] corraz, a hawk, or any bird of prey whose feathers are falling out. Thus in Micah the baldness of the eagle is the time when most of its feathers have dropped out. For although baldness is properly attributed to man, [col. 166] [II, 745] birds too are called bald. Pliny, book 11, chapter 37: Some animals are naturally bald, such as ostriches and water ravens, which among the Greeks take their name from this, that is, οἱ φαλακροκόρακες [hoi phalakrokorakes]. Thus both the Greeks and the Hebrews attribute baldness to birds, differing only in this, that whereas among the Greeks the baldness of birds concerns the head alone, the Hebrews extend it to the whole body; and they call a bird bald which is smooth and stripped of feathers ^{(3)}.

But when others have gradually grown in place of the feathers that fell out, then at last the eagle (in Hebrew נשר) is called מלא הנוצה, full of plumage, and רב נוצה, teeming with plumage. And Scripture indicates in more than one place that feathers grow again in eagles. So in the famous passage of David, Psal. CIII, 5. תתחדש כנשר נעוריכי, You will renew your youth like the eagle. I prefer to render it so with the Chaldee rather than with others, Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's, because the verb תתחדש, of the third person, since it is singular and feminine, agrees neither in gender nor in number with נעוריכי, which is plural and masculine. However that may be, youth is renewed in the eagle in no other way than when new feathers succeed the old, just as a serpent is said to shed its old age when it lays aside its old skin. Hence the Greeks call the slough of a serpent γήρας [gēras], the Romans senium [old age] and senectus [old age]. Thus the words of the Psalmist have the same sense as these of Isaiah, chapter 40, verse 31: Those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength. They shall mount up (grow) feathers like eagles. Where the Seventy elegantly have Πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί [Pterophyēsousin hōs aetoi]. But by a strange metamorphosis the Syriac has transformed the eagles into doves in this version of his, ܢܦܩܘܢ ܓܦܐ ܐܝܟ ܕܝܘܢܐ, They will put forth wings like those of doves. And by no smaller error eagles have been made lions in these words of Theodotion about king Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. IV, 30. var. 33. Αἱ τρίχες αὐτοῦ ὡς λεόντων ἐμεγαλύνθησαν [Hai triches autou hōs leontōn emegalynthēsan]. His hairs grew like those of lions. For in the original it is כנשרין, like those of eagles. But this is an error of the scribes, not of the translator. For no doubt the translator had written ἀετῶν [aetōn], which ignorant scribes changed to λεόντων [leontōn] because αἱ τρίχες [hai triches], that is hairs, did not seem able to fit eagles. So they substituted for eagles the name of a hairy animal, but from a pointless scruple. For in the Prophet's words an analogous word could be supplied: His hairs grew like those of eagles, supply feathers, which are in birds what [II, 746] hairs are in men. Moreover, hairs and locks are sometimes attributed even to birds. By this catachresis Oppian, in book 3 of the Cynegetica, says of the hen that sees a hawk gaping after her chicks,
